patent1998.title: US Patent 5,818,437, "Reduced keyboard disambiguating computer"
patent1998.author: Dale L. Grover, Martin T. King, Clifford A. Kushler
patent1998.quote: Within the memory, the words are stored in order of decreasing frequency of use so that the proper order is automatically presented.
quotes: Within the memory, the words are stored in order of decreasing frequency of use so that the proper order is automatically presented.
Preferably, to save memory, the tag stored in memory 1004 is omitted. Instead, the tag is generated from the content field 1005 whenever the tag is needed for comparison during the search process.

For each search, the system counts the number of letters in the keystroke string, finds the list of words which have that number of letters, calculates the tag for each word, compares the calculated tag to the keystroke string, and sends the word to the display if there is a match.

Vocabulary look-up processing may be handled by a simple binary search. A key field may be generated from text by converting each letter of the text to a number representing the key on which the letter appears. Text records are then stored in memory in sorted order based on this key field.

In the preferred embodiment, the computer includes a standard dictionary so that the sequence of possible words presented to the user is always the same, and the user can commit to rote memory the keystrokes of those words which require two or more strokes of the select key.
Alternatively, the computer can be set to keep track of frequency of usage of words by the user and present first those words most frequently used by the user in his or her distinctive writing style.
A keypad region includes nine data keys 103 and three system-level keys, labeled "select" 104, "0" 105, and "Delete" 106.
When the user presses a letter for the following word, finalizing the selection of the word "Gil", the system automatically adds the new word "Gil" to the user's private vocabulary
supports: granted 6 October 1998; filed 26 July 1995 as application 08/507,756
inventors Dale L. Grover, Martin T. King, Clifford A. Kushler; nine data keys
the ranking is the physical storage order of the on-device dictionary
lookup tags omitted to save memory and regenerated from the stored word during the search
in the preferred embodiment the base dictionary is fixed so the presented order never changes
a separate per-user private vocabulary is layered on top of the fixed base
patent1998.notes: Read from the granted patent PDF front page (https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com/06/c5/ad/38d6e15d1cd6e8/US5818437.pdf) and the Google Patents full text. PDF front page: "11 Patent Number: 5,818,437", "(45) Date of Patent: Oct. 6, 1998", "75 Inventors: Dale L. Grover, Lansing, Mich.; Martin T. King, Vashon, Wash.; Clifford A. Kushler, Wooster, Ohio", "73 Assignee: Tegic Communications, Inc., Seattle, Wash.", "21 Appl. No. 507,756", "22 Filed: Jul. 26, 1995". OWNERSHIP CHAIN, from the USPTO assignment events reproduced on the Google Patents page - this corrects a first-pass error. Google Patents prints a synthesised line "1995-07-26 Application filed by Tegic Communications Inc"; that is an aggregator inference and it is wrong. The recorded assignments are: 1995-07-26 (effective 19950726, reel/frame 007587/0439) GROVER, DALE L. and KUSHLER, CLIFFORD A. assign to KING, MARTIN T.; 1997-12-12 (effective 19961210, reel/frame 008833/0241) security agreement from AIKI CORPORATION to HALEY, JEFFREY T.; 1998-01-13 (effective 19980109, reel/frame 008919/0688) KING, MARTIN T. assigns to TEGIC COMMUNICATIONS, INC.; 1999-10-07 release of security interest; 2014-01-23 TEGIC INC. to NUANCE COMMUNICATIONS, INC. So the application was NOT filed by Tegic in 1995: Tegic took it in January 1998, which is also why the Seattle assignee address printed on the 1998 grant cannot be used to place a 1995 scene, and why Wikipedia's 1996 founding date for Tegic is no longer in conflict. SCOPE: the patent is a "reduced keyboard disambiguating computer" - a portable touch-LCD device with twelve keys, nine of them lettered. The words "telephone", "phone", "cellular" and "mobile" appear nowhere in its specification (only in the cited-reference and citing-patent lists). The handset framing comes from Silfverberg et al. 2000 and MacKenzie & Soukoreff 2002, not from the patent. READ PATH: the patent describes two storage schemes. With tags stored, records sit sorted by key field and look-up "may be handled by a simple binary search". In the preferred, memory-saving scheme the tags are dropped, the words sit in decreasing frequency order, and each search scans the words of matching length regenerating a tag per word. Frequency-as-storage-order and a single-hop lookup are therefore alternatives, not the same design; the story may claim the precomputed order but must not claim a one-hop read path. The preferred embodiment also states the fixed-dictionary rationale, and immediately offers an ALTERNATIVE adaptive mode that reorders by the user's own usage - so "frozen" is the preferred embodiment's choice, not the patent's only option. No ROM/RAM figure appears anywhere in the text.

chi2000.title: Predicting Text Entry Speed on Mobile Phones
chi2000.author: Miika Silfverberg, I. Scott MacKenzie, Panu Korhonen
chi2000.venue: Proceedings of the ACM SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems - CHI 2000, pp. 9-16
chi2000.quote: Of the 9025 words in the sample, 8437 (95%) can be entered and uniquely disambiguated.
quotes: Of the 9025 words in the sample, 8437 (95%) can be entered and uniquely disambiguated.
In a sample of the 9025 most common words in English (ftp://ftp.itri.bton.ac.uk/) produced from the British National Corpus, the user must press NEXT only after about 3% of the words.
Key sequence Initial word Presses of NEXT Subsequent words 2-2-7-3 case 5 care, base, card, bare, cape

Although the T9 dictionary and the disambiguation process are considered proprietary by Tegic, we tested a T9-enabled mobile phone with the key sequences in Figure 8. All the words in Figure 8 were produced, although there were a few minor differences in the sequences.
The initial word for any key sequence is the one with the highest probability in the linguistic model, while subsequent words are produced in decreasing order of their probability.
The T9 input method, patented by Tegic Communications, Inc. (Seattle, WA) [8], uses a dictionary as the basis for disambiguation.
Predicted expert rates vary from 41 wpm for one-handed thumb input to 46 wpm for two-handed index finger input.
supports: 2-2-7-3 yields "case" first, then care, base, card, bare, cape across five NEXT presses (Figure 8)
US 5,818,437 is the T9 patent (reference [8]) and Tegic was in Seattle by 2000
chi2000.notes: Venue-drift guard: read from the PDF title page, which reads 'Predicting Text Entry Speed on Mobile Phones' (singular 'Speed'). MacKenzie's own publication list renders the title with the plural 'speeds'. The PDF running head reads 'CHI 2000 - 1-6 APRIL 2000 - Papers'. Author affiliations on the PDF: Nokia Research Center (Silfverberg, Korhonen) and York University, Dept. of Mathematics & Statistics (MacKenzie). ATTRIBUTION GUARD: the 9025/8437 figure is an analysis over the authors' own word sample (the 9025 most common English words from the British National Corpus), not a measurement of T9's shipped dictionary, which the paper says Tegic treats as proprietary. Figure 8 is captioned 'Examples of ambiguous words for T9' and the authors did check its sequences on a T9-enabled phone: all the words were produced, 'although there were a few minor differences in the sequences'. Do not write that they 'tested T9' against 9025 words. The paper is also internally inconsistent on the NEXT rate (about 3% in the text, 5% adopted as the working figure, while Figure 7's counts 476+83+23+5+1 = 588 of 9025 give 6.5%); only the quoted 8437 (95%) figure is used here. Reference [8] misspells the third inventor 'Kuschler'; the patent itself prints 'Clifford A. Kushler'. Re-check aid: the headline quote spans the page 5/6 break ('...Of the 9025' | 'words in the sample, 8437 (95%)...'), and the paper is two-column, so 'pdftotext -layout' interleaves the columns; extract without -layout.

hci2002.title: Text Entry for Mobile Computing: Models and Methods, Theory and Practice
hci2002.author: I. Scott MacKenzie, R. William Soukoreff
hci2002.quote: This greatly reduces the memory requirements of the implementation—a critical factor for mobile phones.
quotes: This greatly reduces the memory requirements of the implementation—a critical factor for mobile phones.
Disambiguation technology takes key press sequences and uses an embedded database of language statistics to identify legal words.

T9 compares the word possibilities to a linguistic database to guess the intended word. Naturally, linguistic disambiguation is not perfect because multiple words may have the same key sequence. In these cases the most common word is the default.
supports: on-device dictionary size was a hard constraint on 1990s handsets
hci2002.notes: Read from the PDF, whose front matter reads 'HUMAN-COMPUTER INTERACTION, 2002, Volume 17, pp. 147-198, Copyright 2002, Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Inc.' The quoted clause sits in the paragraph describing WordWise's mode shift (which lets explicit words be omitted from the internal database) and is a general statement about handset memory, not a measurement of T9's dictionary. The story uses it only as evidence that on-device memory was the binding constraint, never as a number for T9. The published text uses an em dash, reproduced here.

aol10k.title: America Online, Inc., Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2000
aol10k.author: America Online, Inc.
aol10k.quote: In November 1999, the Company completed its merger with Tegic Communications, Inc. ("Tegic"), in which Tegic became a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Company. The Company exhanged approximately 4.8 million shares of common stock for all the outstanding common and preferred shares of Tegic in a transaction that was accounted for as a pooling-of-interests.
quotes: In November 1999, the Company completed its merger with Tegic Communications, Inc. ("Tegic"), in which Tegic became a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Company. The Company exhanged approximately 4.8 million shares of common stock for all the outstanding common and preferred shares of Tegic in a transaction that was accounted for as a pooling-of-interests.
In December 1999, the Company recorded a charge of approximately $5 million of direct costs related to the merger of Tegic Communications, Inc. ("Tegic").
Tegic has it operations in Seattle, Washington.

AOL Wireless also provides text entry solutions for wireless devices through the Company's subsidiary, Tegic Communications, Inc. Tegic's leading product, the T9 Text Input software, enables individuals to send e-mail, short messaging services and instant messages, as well as perform other text-based functions and access the Internet, using the standard telephone keypad to enter words or sentences.
supports: consideration was approximately 4.8 million AOL shares, pooling-of-interests
aol10k.notes: Read from the EDGAR filing text; cover page reads 'For the fiscal year ended June 30, 2000'. Vendor-PR guard: press coverage and the allocation brief put the price at roughly $300M-$350M in stock. AOL's own 10-K states no dollar figure and gives approximately 4.8 million shares; the story uses the filing's number, not the press figure. Date guard: press reports date the deal 3 December 1999; AOL's 10-K says the merger completed in November 1999 and books a separate $5M charge in December 1999. Two typos in the original filing are quoted verbatim: 'exhanged' and 'Tegic has it operations'. This filing places Tegic in Seattle in 2000, not in 1995.

unverified: The exact ROM or RAM budget, in kilobytes, of the handsets T9 first shipped on. No primary source read here states a figure; the patent describes omitting stored lookup tags 'to save memory' without quantifying the saving. The patent never uses the words ROM, RAM, read-only or nonvolatile anywhere in its text, so which kind of memory the omitted tags saved is unverified too; the prose says only "memory".
The dollar value of the AOL-Tegic deal. Press reports give roughly $300M and roughly $350M in stock; AOL's 10-K gives only a share count. No dollar figure appears in the prose.
The total number of handsets T9 ultimately shipped on. Commonly given as 'billions' with no primary source; not claimed in the prose.
The claim that T9 stands for 'Text on 9 keys'. Asserted uncited on Wikipedia; not found in the patent, the CHI 2000 paper or the AOL 10-K, and not used in the prose or on any card.

Where Grover, King and Kushler actually worked in 1995, and whether they worked together in one place. The granted patent gives three separate inventor addresses (Lansing, Michigan; Vashon, Washington; Wooster, Ohio) and the Seattle assignee address dates from the January 1998 assignment to Tegic, not from the filing. The first draft of this story was tagged 'Seattle, 1995' on that basis; the tag is now 'USPTO, 1995' and no 1995 location is claimed.

Tegic's founding year and its relationship to AIKI Corporation, which granted a security interest in this patent effective December 1996. Wikipedia gives Tegic as founded in Seattle in 1996. Not claimed anywhere in the prose or cards.

The exact size of the per-device user dictionary on shipped handsets, and whether it survived a device reset. The patent describes a 'private vocabulary' mechanism but gives no capacity, and no primary source for shipped behaviour was found.

Whether T9's shipped dictionary was in fact ordered from a text corpus. The patent says only 'decreasing frequency of use'; the CHI 2000 sample is British National Corpus derived but is the authors' sample, not Tegic's. The prose's one use of 'corpus' rests on this inference.

Whether the version of the design that shipped on phones used the patent's preferred scan-with-regenerated-tags scheme or its stored-tag binary search. The patent describes both; no source read here says which shipped.
